summary: Defines jCal, a JSON format for iCalendar data. iCalendar is the text format for events and tasks in calendar applications, and JSON is a common lightweight data format.

plainLanguage.summary: jCal is a way to write calendar data, such as events and tasks, as JSON. Every part of an iCalendar file has a matching JSON shape, so the same calendar can be sent as either format without losing information.

questions: how does jcal represent icalendar properties
what is the jcal media type
how are recurrence rules written in jcal
subtitle: A one-to-one mapping that lets calendar events and tasks travel as ordinary JSON arrays and objects.

tldr.problem: iCalendar is a specialised text format that needs its own parser, while JSON is the format that JavaScript libraries and web widgets already handle.
tldr.mechanism: jCal maps every iCalendar component to a three-element array, every property to an array of name, parameters, type and values, and every parameter to a JSON object.
tldr.outcome: Calendar data can be converted to JSON and back without losing meaning. RFC 7265 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 7529.

facts.label: Property array
facts.value: 3 fixed elements plus one or more values

today: RFC 7265 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014. It was later updated by RFC 7529, which added recurrence rules for non-Gregorian calendars, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why jCal Exists
sections.content:
iCalendar is a widely deployed interchange format for calendaring and scheduling data. Many applications and services read and write calendar data, but iCalendar is a specialised text format that requires its own parser and generator. JSON, by contrast, is the native format for JavaScript widgets and libraries, and it is appropriate to have a standard form of calendar data that is easier to work with.

jCal is defined as a straightforward mapping from iCalendar into JSON, so that iCalendar data can be converted to JSON and then back to iCalendar without losing any semantic meaning. Anyone who creates jCal data according to the specification knows their data can be converted to a valid iCalendar representation as well.

The design considerations are the same as those for RFC 6321, which defines xCal for XML:

  • Round-tripping an iCalendar instance through jCal gives the same semantic result, and all components, properties and property parameters are preserved.
  • The order of elements and the case of property and parameter names are not necessarily preserved.
  • The iCalendar semantics are preserved, so a simple consumer can browse the data in jCal, although a full understanding of iCalendar is still needed to modify it.
  • Extensions to the underlying iCalendar specification must not lead to a need to update jCal.
sections.plainLanguage: Calendar data is usually written in a format called iCalendar, which is a text format with its own rules. Many programs work better with JSON, the format used by web pages. jCal defines exactly how each piece of an iCalendar file becomes a piece of JSON, and back again.

sections.title: Components, Properties and Parameters
sections.content:
An iCalendar object is made of components, properties, parameters and values. A component can hold other components or properties. A property has a value and a set of zero or more parameters.

Each component becomes a three-element array. The first element is the component name in lowercase, the second is an array of the properties that belong to it, and the third is an array of its sub-components. The mapping is the same for the top level object and for every sub-component, and it stays valid for components added to iCalendar in the future.

Each property becomes an array with three fixed elements followed by one or more values. The fixed elements are the property name in lowercase, an object holding the parameters, and the type identifier of the value in lowercase. A single-valued property therefore has exactly four elements, and a multi-valued property has one element per value. Because some properties are special-cased, a parser must check both the type identifier and the data type rather than assume a type from the property name.

Parameters become a JSON object in which each key is a parameter name in lowercase and each value is the parameter value with its original case preserved. A parameter that holds a comma-separated list becomes an array of strings; a single-value parameter may be written either as one string or as an array with one string, and a parser must accept both. The quotation marks that iCalendar requires around parameter values containing a colon, a semicolon or a comma are not part of the value and are dropped.

The VALUE parameter is never stored in the parameter object. The value type is signalled by the type identifier in the third element of the property array instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Every component becomes an array of three things: its name, its properties, and any components inside it. Every property becomes an array holding its name, its parameters, its value type, and the value itself. Parameters go into a JSON object with lower-case names.

sections.title: Value Types
sections.content:
Each iCalendar value type has its own jCal type identifier and its own JSON form.

  • binary is a JSON string encoded with base64, as in RFC 4648.
  • boolean is a JSON boolean, and float and integer are JSON numbers.
  • cal-address and uri are JSON strings holding a URI as described in RFC 3986.
  • text is a JSON string.
  • date, date-time and time are JSON strings in the complete representation of RFC 5545, written using the extended format of ISO 8601. Other variations, such as reduced accuracy, MUST NOT be used.
  • duration is a JSON string holding the same duration value as iCalendar.
  • utc-offset is a JSON string, with the hour and minute separated by a colon, such as -05:00.
  • period is an array of two JSON strings: the start of the period as a date-time, and the end as either a date-time or a duration.
  • recur is an object describing a recurrence rule. Each rule part is a key-value pair whose key is the lower-case name of the part. The freq and wkst values are strings with case preserved, until is a date or date-time, count and interval are single numbers, and the parts that may repeat, such as bymonthday or byday, use an array when they hold more than one value.

Two properties have special forms. The geo property holds an array of two values, latitude first and longitude second. The request-status property holds an array of two or three strings: a code, a description, and optional extra data.

Extension properties and parameters, the ones whose names start with X-, are handled the same way as ordinary ones, with the name in lowercase, so X-FOO becomes x-foo.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of calendar value has a matching JSON form. Dates and times use the full ISO 8601 layout, so a date reads like 2011-05-17. A repeating rule becomes a JSON object with one entry per rule part.

sections.title: Converting Between the Formats
sections.content:
iCalendar folds long lines to keep them within a maximum line length, typically 75 octets, and it escapes certain characters in text values and parameter values. When converting from iCalendar to jCal, the lines MUST first be unfolded, then the iCalendar escaping MUST be unescaped, and finally the JSON escaping described in RFC 7159 MUST be applied. The reverse order applies when converting from jCal to iCalendar.

iCalendar uses base64 for binary data but does not stop that encoding being applied to other value types. When a property carries the ENCODING parameter set to BASE64, the base64 encoding MUST be preserved if the value type is BINARY; otherwise the ENCODING parameter MUST be removed and the value MUST be base64 decoded. Non-binary value types MUST NOT be base64 encoded when converting back to iCalendar.

When converting back, component, property and parameter names SHOULD be converted to uppercase, JSON escaping is unescaped, iCalendar escaping is applied, and long lines SHOULD be folded. The VALUE parameter MUST be added to properties whose default value type is unknown but whose jCal type identifier is not unknown, and it MUST be omitted for properties with the unknown type identifier.

iCalendar data can be a stream of several objects, but jCal has no equivalent for a stream. To transport several jCal objects, a plain JSON array is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Converting to JSON means unfolding wrapped lines, undoing the calendar escaping, then applying normal JSON escaping. Converting back runs those steps in reverse and wraps long lines again.

sections.title: Unrecognized Properties and Parameters
sections.content:
A converter may meet a property it does not recognise, or one whose default value type it does not know. To keep such data intact across a round trip, jCal introduces a new unknown value type. This specification reserves the UNKNOWN value data type in iCalendar: it MUST NOT be used in iCalendar or in any extension to it, and it is registered in the iCalendar Data Types registry with the status "Reserved - Do not use".

When converting iCalendar into jCal, any property that has no VALUE parameter and whose default value type is not known MUST be converted to a primitive JSON string holding the unprocessed value text, with the value type set to unknown. Using text instead is called out as harmful, because it can apply extra escaping and break the round trip. Any unrecognised property parameter MUST be converted to a string value holding the parameter value text, treated as if it were a TEXT value.

When converting jCal back into iCalendar, the value type is always explicit and is passed through the VALUE parameter, except that the parameter MAY be omitted when the type matches the iCalendar default, and it MUST NOT be used when the type is unknown, in which case the value is taken over without any processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Some calendar properties are new to the program doing the conversion. To keep them unchanged, jCal marks them with the type name unknown and leaves the text alone. That way the same text comes back on the way out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This specification defines how iCalendar data is translated between two formats with a one-to-one mapping, so that all the semantic data is preserved in both. It does not change the meaning of the underlying data, and it neither imposes nor removes any security considerations that apply to that data.

JSON has its own inherent security risks, as described in Section 12 of RFC 7159. Even though JSON is considered a safe subset of JavaScript, a flaw in the parser processing JSON could still impose a threat that does not arise with conventional iCalendar data. A parser for jCal should therefore be aware of the security implications. The use of JavaScript's eval() function is called out as an unacceptable security risk, and a native parser with full awareness of the JSON format is preferred.

The document also expects this format to spread iCalendar data more widely, for example in web applications rather than only in dedicated calendaring applications. In all cases, application developers have to conform to the semantics of the iCalendar data as defined in RFC 5545 and its extensions, and the security considerations in Section 7 of that document apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The format adds no new risks to calendar data itself, but JSON parsers have their own weaknesses, so a program should use a proper JSON parser and never hand the text to eval.

sections.title: Media Type and Registrations
sections.content:
The document defines a MIME media type for iCalendar data in JSON. The type name is application and the subtype name is calendar+json. There are no required parameters. The optional parameters are method, component and optinfo, as defined for the text/calendar media type. The encoding considerations are the same as for application/json, and the intended usage is COMMON with no restrictions on where the type can be used.

The media type is offered as an alternative: applications that use text/calendar can use this instead, and applications that use application/json to transfer calendaring data can use this type to say more about the content.

IANA has also added the UNKNOWN entry to the iCalendar Data Types registry. Its purpose is to allow preserving property values whose default value type is not known during round-tripping between jCal and iCalendar. It is reserved for the exclusive use of the jCal format, and the registry entry says "Reserved - Do not use".
sections.plainLanguage: The document registers a media type, application/calendar+json, so that programs can say they are sending calendar data as JSON. It also reserves the word unknown so that no other calendar format uses it.
